means:
Without flavour; by extension, without interest, character, or spark.

The word is a sneer. *Mild* and *plain* are neutral descriptions; **insipid** is a verdict — it says the thing *should* have had flavour and failed to deliver any. It works on soup, on prose, on a melody, on a person, and in every case it implies the critic tasted carefully and found nothing there. Slightly more literary and more withering than *boring*: you call a lecture boring, you call a novel insipid.
trap: ⚠️ **insipid ≠ insidious.** Both open *in-si-*, and there the resemblance ends: **insipid** = flavourless, dull; **insidious** = creeping and treacherous, harmful by stealth. An insipid remark bores you; an insidious one damages you quietly.
trick_line: **in-SIP-id** — take a **sip**, taste nothing, and say so with a curl of the lip.
trick_unpack: The hidden *sip* fixes the tasting metaphor, and the curled lip fixes the contempt that separates *insipid* from a neutral word like *mild*.
sentences: Reviewers dismissed the novel as an **insipid** imitation of far braver books.
The tea was **insipid** — basically hot water with ambitions.
in_the_wild: Standard wine- and food-critic vocabulary: an **insipid** wine is one with no acid, no fruit, nothing to say — the polite word for "watery."
etymology:
Latin **in-** (*not*) + **sapidus** (*tasty*), from **sapere** = *"to taste"* — and, because taste and judgement were one idea to the Romans, also *"to be wise."*

That double sense pays out across the exam: **sapid** (full of flavour), **savour**, **savoury**, **sage**, **sapient**, **Homo sapiens** — the "wise" ape, literally the one with taste.
one_line: Bland to the point of dullness; flavourless, in food or people.
